leadIn.title: Lead-In & Context: Countable & Uncountable Nouns
leadIn.content: In the kitchen: We have three apples and some bread. Some food items can be counted, while others are measured as a mass.

meaningCheck.question: Function check: What is the primary purpose of using Countable & Uncountable Nouns?
options: To express clear, level-appropriate meaning in structured context
To translate sentences word-for-word from another language
It is an obsolete form never used by native speakers
meaningCheck.explanation: Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.

meaningCheck.question: Form check: Does correct usage of Countable & Uncountable Nouns require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
options: No, agreement rules are optional in English
Yes, matching grammatical forms ensures natural, accurate communication
Agreement only matters in formal academic writing
meaningCheck.explanation: Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.

form.title: Form & Structure: Countable & Uncountable Nouns
form.content: Countable: singular (an apple) / plural (two apples). Uncountable: no plural form, use 'some/water/milk' without 'a/an'.

pronunciation.title: Pronunciation Notes: Countable & Uncountable Nouns
pronunciation.content: Spoken stress, weak forms, intonation, and articulation patterns for Countable & Uncountable Nouns.

controlledPractice.question: Which is uncountable?
controlledPractice.explanation: Water has no plural form and can't be counted directly · it's uncountable.

controlledPractice.question: 'She has three ___.' (information)
controlledPractice.explanation: Use a container word to count uncountable nouns: pieces of information.

controlledPractice.question: 'How ___ apples do you have?'
controlledPractice.explanation: Many is used with countable plural nouns.
